title: Justify a design pattern from a recurring problem, constraints and variation point and distinguish its intent and cost from a similar implementation shape

questions.prompt:
An app depends on its own interface `IFraudCheck`, which has one method: `Score(Order order)` returning a risk value from 0 to 1. The team must now use a third-party fraud service. Its SDK cannot be changed. It exposes `Evaluate(string customerId, decimal amount, string currency)` and returns a text verdict: `"low"`, `"medium"` or `"high"`. Several parts of the app already call `IFraudCheck`.

Which design pattern fits this situation? Justify the choice from the design pressure and constraints in the scenario.

rubric.point: Identifies Adapter, either object or class form, as the pattern.

Justifies it from the pressure: the vendor's interface does not match the contract the consumers expect, and the vendor side cannot be changed or aligned directly. The pattern therefore keeps the translation of arguments and results in one place, so existing callers of `IFraudCheck` stay unchanged.

questions.model: **Adapter.** The SDK's interface does not match `IFraudCheck`, and the SDK cannot be changed, so the two contracts cannot be aligned directly. An adapter implements `IFraudCheck`, translates an `Order` into the SDK's arguments and converts the text verdict back into a score. That keeps the translation at one boundary, and existing callers do not change.

source.heading: Choose a Pattern by Intent and Cost

questions.prompt: A class `GuardedReportStore` implements the same `IReportStore` interface as `SqlReportStore` and holds a reference to it. For each call, it checks the current user's role. If the role is allowed, it forwards the call unchanged to `SqlReportStore`. If not, it throws an exception without calling the real store. Which pattern does this class implement, and why?
options: Decorator, because it keeps the same interface and stacks a new responsibility around every call to the wrapped store.
Proxy, because it keeps the same interface and decides whether each call is allowed to reach the real store.
Adapter, because it sits between callers and the store and converts their calls into operations the store accepts.
Strategy, because it delegates to another object that supplies an interchangeable way of performing the operation.

rubric.point: Chooses Proxy because the wrapper keeps the same interface and controls access by deciding whether a call reaches the real object.

questions.model: **Proxy.** The wrapper has the same interface as the real store, and its job is to control access by forwarding or refusing each call. A Decorator would add behavior while the call normally still reaches the wrapped object. An Adapter would translate between different interfaces.

source.heading: Choose a Pattern by Intent and Cost

c1.text: I assume the adapter could fit, which will translate new third-party service to the established app contracts

annotations.quote: I assume the adapter could fit
annotations.note: You identified Adapter, which is the right pattern for this scenario.

annotations.quote: translate new third-party service to the established app contracts
annotations.note: This gestures at translating to the existing contract, but it doesn't say why Adapter is needed. You didn't mention that the SDK can't be changed, or that existing `IFraudCheck` callers stay untouched.
The justification needs the design pressure: the vendor's interface mismatches `IFraudCheck` and can't be modified. Translation is then kept in one place, so existing callers don't change.

c1.feedback: Adapter is correct, but the justification doesn't cite the unchangeable SDK or the unchanged callers of `IFraudCheck`.
